thesis: Prospective-memory reliability requires four explicit runtime boundaries: versioned intention state, observation policy, due/action admission, and effect evidence.
argument: PM-Bench separates retrospective recall from acting at a future cue and makes active-versus-due state explicit.
Source-reported results show no universal best scaffold; aggressive monitoring can add queries and false positives without yielding the best F1.
Cancellation, override, rescheduling and hidden-channel triggers imply a lifecycle and observation problem that a plain memory record does not solve.
A governed runtime can therefore preserve model intelligence while externalizing future authority into auditable intention, observation, admission and effect records.
counterarguments: the model alone should decide due state
nonClaims: PM-Bench does not prove the proposed four-boundary architecture.
COLM publication is not independent validation.
The run does not claim production safety or exactly-once semantics were benchmarked.
